rows.why: The tools and MCP servers the AI can call, hosted inside or used from outside, are identified with who runs each and what third-party software it brings.
Internal controls for each tool or MCP server (approval before use, permission limits, allowed versions) are identified and documented.
The scope of what each tool can read, write and do, and the credentials it uses, is specified against what the use case needs.
The outside networks, servers and upstream systems the AI's tools connect to, and how data flows to them, are documented.
The likelihood and size of harm from tool misuse (injected instructions, over-broad permissions, a compromised outside server) are assessed.
Tools and MCP servers are tested for security, including prompt injection driving tool calls, permission abuse and a malicious or changed server.
Tool calls are logged with the credentials used and what was done, so actions can be traced and accounted for.
Tool use in production is monitored for unexpected calls, new capabilities on a known server and unusual volume.
The privacy risk of data flowing through tools to MCP servers and outside services is examined, including what leaves and to whom.
Controls that keep tool use within bounds in practice (permissions narrower than the user's, short-lived credentials, gateway enforcement, rate limits) are applied and kept working.
A tool or MCP incident (misused credential, injected call, compromised server) has a response and recovery procedure that is followed.
A tool, credential or MCP server can be switched off or revoked quickly, with an owner assigned, when it misbehaves.
Outside MCP servers and tool suppliers are monitored regularly and their risk controls applied and documented.
Post-deployment monitoring of tools covers change management for new tools or permissions, review of use, and decommissioning of unused tools.
Tool incidents and errors are recorded, communicated to those affected, and followed up after recovery.

review.reason: The why's 'permission limits' repeats MAP 3.3 (scope and credentials) and MANAGE 2.2 (permissions kept within bounds), and MCP-6.8 is reused in all three; narrow it to approval before use and allowed versions.
'Review of use' repeats the MEASURE 2.4 check on production tool use (same MCP-8.11); keep only change management for new tools or permissions and decommissioning.
Nothing asks which tool actions (writes, deletes, payments, external sends) need a human to confirm before they run; MCP-17.4 itself mentions human confirmation enforcement.
Nothing checks that the AI fails safely when a tool or MCP server errors, times out, is unavailable or returns something unexpected, rather than retrying or taking partial changes.
